article_title: OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching
citation: Hao Liang, Qihan Lin, Meiyi Qiang, Linzhuang Sun, Hengyi Feng, Mingrui Chen, Sizhe Qiu, Wentao Zhang. (2026). OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23088
title: Four-capability taxonomy for organizing educational foundation-model supervision
description: OmniEdu organizes education-specific supervision around four complementary capability categories defined "according to the behaviors to be learned" rather than by source or subject. Subject competence covers solving K-12 problems and explaining answers across mathematics, science, reading, and writing; curriculum grounding captures grade-level alignment, knowledge points, prerequisite relations, and difficulty; diagnostic reasoning targets identifying errors and misconceptions and inferring missing prerequisites; pedagogical action and scaffolding covers selecting and executing interventions such as hints, questions, prerequisite review, or direct explanation. The taxonomy provides a common language for both data construction and evaluation.
requirements: Each example is assigned to a single primary capability according to its main supervision objective, with other properties retained as secondary metadata.
constraints: The taxonomy is designed for K-12 educational scenarios and is implemented through fine-grained task buckets within each capability.
examples: The final corpus allocates 45.5% of examples to subject competence, 20.3% to pedagogical action and scaffolding, 13.4% to curriculum grounding, and 7.8% to diagnostic reasoning, plus 12.9% general-purpose instruction.
key_sources: Hao Liang, Qihan Lin, Meiyi Qiang, Linzhuang Sun, Hengyi Feng, Mingrui Chen, Sizhe Qiu, Wentao Zhang. (2026). OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23088

article_title: OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching
citation: Hao Liang, Qihan Lin, Meiyi Qiang, Linzhuang Sun, Hengyi Feng, Mingrui Chen, Sizhe Qiu, Wentao Zhang. (2026). OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23088
title: OmniEdu capability-oriented instruction-tuning corpus and six-stage data pipeline
description: A reproducible data-construction pipeline that curates an education-specific pool of approximately 1.34M examples drawn from more than 100 datasets and educational resources into 60,951 high-quality examples containing about 12.0M supervised response tokens. The six stages combine deterministic cleaning and evaluation decontamination, LLM-assisted semantic auditing and rewriting with 0-100 usability scoring, task-specific quality scoring, k-center greedy diversity selection over BGE-M3 embeddings under token budgets, and pedagogical instruction assignment. Together with 9,048 general-purpose examples, the final corpus contains 69,999 examples and 15.96M supervised response tokens, with provenance and audit metadata retained throughout.
requirements: Source and license information is retained for provenance tracking, and data with unclear usage conditions are excluded.
constraints: Examples overlapping the final evaluation set are removed to prevent evaluation contamination; rewritten examples are retained only if re-audited as keep.
examples: RACE is reduced from 60,180 to 5,000 examples via k-center greedy selection; auditing retains examples scoring 85-100, repairs those scoring 50-84, and discards those below 50.
key_sources: Hao Liang, Qihan Lin, Meiyi Qiang, Linzhuang Sun, Hengyi Feng, Mingrui Chen, Sizhe Qiu, Wentao Zhang. (2026). OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23088

article_title: Tracing and Pointing Support Multimedia Learning: A Cross-Cultural Replication
citation: Yining Wang, Kexin Han, Paul Ginns. (2025). Tracing and Pointing Support Multimedia Learning: A Cross-Cultural Replication. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10005-7
title: Give learners omnibus pre-lesson instructions offering multiple hand-action options rather than one restricted action
description: When multimedia lessons require learners to connect text and diagram elements, the article recommends "omnibus" pre-lesson instructions that offer several touch-based options — pointing, leaving a finger on the diagram, using both hands, tracing arrows — rather than a single restricted action. The authors argue such combined instructions "appear to support learning more than more restricted (one-handed) actions on lesson materials", based on a comparison with recent studies that restricted learners to pointing or tracing alone. The present study's instruction sheet modelled this omnibus approach.
requirements: Lesson materials combining expository text with diagrams so that hand actions can link related elements
constraints: The recommendation contrasts this study's combined instructions with computer-based studies using restricted actions; it is the authors' comparative interpretation, not a manipulation tested within this experiment
target_learners: adult learners studying multimedia expository lessons
target_learning_goals: integrating textual and diagrammatic information in multimedia lessons
examples: The instruction sheet offered four options: point at text and corresponding diagram location, leave a finger on the diagram while reading, use more than one finger/hand, and trace along arrows indicating blood flow
key_sources: Yining Wang, Kexin Han, Paul Ginns. (2025). Tracing and Pointing Support Multimedia Learning: A Cross-Cultural Replication. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10005-7

article_title: Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives
citation: Mizoguchi, R., & Bourdeau, J. (2015). Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0077-5
title: OMNIBUS: an ontology of learning/instructional theories as ways of goal decomposition
description: OMNIBUS is an ontology of learning/instructional theories built with the Hozo editor, capturing theories "as a set of ways of decomposing a goal into a sequence of sub-goals". The article reports that "OMNIBUS has 99 ways of goal decomposition extracted from 11 theories/models", for example decomposing 'to help learners learn' differently under behaviorist versus constructivist approaches. It is described as the framework able to include any theory compliant with its specifications of theory and model.
requirements: Theories and models must comply with the specification of the concepts of theory and of model to be included
constraints: Building on OMNIBUS requires mastering a high-complexity system and the Hozo editor, which the authors name as obstacles to adoption
target_learners: Authors of intelligent tutoring systems and instructional designers
examples: A behaviorist way of instruction is modeled as decomposing the goal into giving stimuli, observing the response, and repeating
key_sources: Mizoguchi, R., & Bourdeau, J. (2015). Using Ontological Engineering to Overcome AI-ED Problems: Contribution, Impact and Perspectives. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0077-5

citation: Devedzic, V. (2016). Not Fade Away? Commentary to paper Education and The Semantic Web (IJAIED Vol.14, 2004). International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 378–386. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0051-2
title: OMNIBUS ontology of learning, instruction and instructional design and the SMARTIES authoring system
description: OMNIBUS is an ontology of learning, instruction and instructional design built over years by Riichiro Mizoguchi, Jacqueline Bourdeau and their students and associates. On top of it sits SMARTIES, described by the article as "the world-first authoring system that helps authors develop theory-compliant learning scenarios". The commentary cites both as among the best-known research efforts in educational ontologies.
requirements: Ontological engineering to organize learning and instructional theories
constraints: The commentary notes such efforts were ahead of their time and too advanced to become popular with ordinary researchers or industry
target_learners: authors of learning scenarios and instructional designers
examples: Hayashi, Bourdeau and Mizoguchi (2009) built SMARTIES on top of OMNIBUS
key_sources: Devedzic, V. (2016). Not Fade Away? Commentary to paper Education and The Semantic Web (IJAIED Vol.14, 2004). International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 378–386. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0051-2

article_title: Orientation and Mobility Training in Special Education Curriculum for Social Adjustment Problems of Visually Impaired Children in Pakistan
citation: Malik, S., Abd Manaf, U. K., Ahmad, N. A., & Ismail, M. (2018). Orientation and Mobility Training in Special Education Curriculum for Social Adjustment Problems of Visually Impaired Children in Pakistan. International Journal of Instruction, 11(2), 185-202. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11213a
title: The O&M curriculum: mobility techniques, devices and the Expanded Core Curriculum
description: The O&M curriculum is a planned teaching system, part of the Expanded Core Curriculum for visually impaired learners, that teaches independent and confident movement using other senses and equipment. The article states "The regular O&M syllabi include various techniques related to mobility skills. These techniques are guidi ng technique, long cane technique, traveling tactics, searching for destination and using public transport". It also lists devices such as optical devices, electronic travel aids and global positioning systems, and major training foci including perceptual skills, environmental knowledge, sensory and motor development.
requirements: Qualified O&M specialists must conduct O&M assessments for students with visual impairments, ideally early and before prior evaluation lapses, per the article
constraints: The article notes little research exists on the O&M skill levels and specific training needs of children with low vision
target_learners: visually impaired children aged 5-15 in special education institutes
examples: The study measured O&M training as delivered in special education institutes with an 11-item scale adapted from the TAPS questionnaire used in NLTS2
key_sources: Malik, S., Abd Manaf, U. K., Ahmad, N. A., & Ismail, M. (2018). Orientation and Mobility Training in Special Education Curriculum for Social Adjustment Problems of Visually Impaired Children in Pakistan. International Journal of Instruction, 11(2), 185-202. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11213a

article_title: Video-enhanced training for entrustable professional activities in preclinical oral surgery: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Lin Yue, Wen Zhe, Li Yuqi, Wei Xiaosong, Zhang Jiafen, Yan Tinglin, Bao Zhexuan. (2025). Video-enhanced training for entrustable professional activities in preclinical oral surgery: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08368-0
title: Validated 23-item OMFS-EPA assessment scale with self- and teacher-evaluation components weighted 50% each
description: A customized EPA scoring rubric for preclinical oral surgery built around tooth extraction, with operation-process (80 points) and operation-outcome (20 points) sections, each item weighted equally across self- and teacher evaluation. Content validity came from a two-round Delphi review in which "the final 23 items achieved an I-CVI of 0.81–0.94 and an S-CVI/Ave of 0.94". Internal consistency was Cronbach's alpha 0.91 (self-assessment) and 0.92 (teacher evaluation), with inter-rater ICC 0.87 after a two-hour calibration session (pre-assessment video ICC 0.86).
requirements: Calibrated raters; the study used a two-hour rubric review and standardized video scoring session before formal assessment
constraints: The article states psychometric properties require more validation via larger, multi-institution cohorts, confirmatory factor analysis, and predictive validity work
target_learners: Undergraduate dental students in preclinical OMFS training
target_learning_goals: EPA-related competency assessment: communication, history taking, examination, operational skills, health education, and humanistic care
examples: The scale was scored by three blinded senior attending physicians from another campus; self-evaluation and faculty evaluation each contribute 50% to the final score
key_sources: Lin Yue, Wen Zhe, Li Yuqi, Wei Xiaosong, Zhang Jiafen, Yan Tinglin, Bao Zhexuan. (2025). Video-enhanced training for entrustable professional activities in preclinical oral surgery: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08368-0

article_title: Efficacy of modified team-based learning in a flipped classroom for an acute-care nursing course: A mixed-methods study.
citation: Murata, H., Asakawa, S., Kawamura, T., Yamauchi, H., Takahashi, O., & Henker, R. (2023). Efficacy of modified team‐based learning in a flipped classroom for an acute‐care nursing course: A mixed‐methods study. Nursing Open, 10, 4786–4796. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.1730
title: Remove the peer evaluation step from team-based learning when implementing TBL with Japanese nursing students, and team-approach gains are still obtained
description: The article removed peer evaluation—the final step of the original US version of TBL—because Japanese learners were reported to be reluctant to engage in it and uncomfortable appraising peers, concerns linked to traditionally valued harmony and avoidance of friction. In the M-TBL intervention without this step, team approach scores still increased significantly across time-points, and groups both for and against peer evaluation improved, indicating the step can be omitted without losing the team-building benefit.
requirements: An alternative evaluation structure, such as unified teacher rubrics scoring the team's case materials, case assessment and nursing plan
constraints: Removing peer evaluation leaves perceived unfairness in unequal member contribution unresolved, which the authors say may require a more robust evaluation system
target_learning_goals: Team approach development without socio-emotional discomfort from peer appraisal
examples: The intervention replaced peer evaluation with final evaluation of group work by three teachers using unified rubrics, accounting for 20% of students' final grade
key_sources: Murata, H., Asakawa, S., Kawamura, T., Yamauchi, H., Takahashi, O., & Henker, R. (2023). Efficacy of modified team‐based learning in a flipped classroom for an acute‐care nursing course: A mixed‐methods study. Nursing Open, 10, 4786–4796. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.1730

article_title: Development and Evaluation of a Preceptor Education Program Based on the One-Minute Preceptor Model: Participatory Action Research.
citation: Jeong Hye Won, Ju Deok, Choi Myoung Lee, Kim Suhyun. (2021). Development and Evaluation of a Preceptor Education Program Based on the One-Minute Preceptor Model: Participatory Action Research. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph182111376
title: OMP-based preceptor education program (PEP) developed through participatory action research
description: An eight-week preceptor education program developed and applied with 30 preceptor nurses at a Korean tertiary hospital through participatory action research. It comprised two weeks of developing standardized nursing practice standards (content validity index ≥0.80 required) followed by six weekly application sessions, with daily conferences by education specialist nurses, weekly reflection journals, mini lectures, and facilitator support from four researchers and four education specialist nurses. Quantitative evaluation showed no significant CCCP or GICC-15 change, while qualitative analysis documented growth experiences.
requirements: Facilitators (researchers and education specialist nurses) supporting weekly conferences
Organizational support including a training room and nursing department cooperation
constraints: Conducted at tertiary general hospitals in one region of Korea; the authors state generalizability is limited and there was no control group
target_learners: preceptor nurses with at least three years of clinical experience
examples: Education specialist nurses conducted a systematic literature review and developed nursing practice standards with continuous modification by preceptor nurses
key_sources: Jeong Hye Won, Ju Deok, Choi Myoung Lee, Kim Suhyun. (2021). Development and Evaluation of a Preceptor Education Program Based on the One-Minute Preceptor Model: Participatory Action Research. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph182111376

article_title: Computerized Sign Language-Based Literacy Training for Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Children.
citation: Holmer Emil, Heimann Mikael, Rudner Mary. (2017). Computerized Sign Language-Based Literacy Training for Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Children. The Journal of Deaf Studies and Deaf Education. https://doi.org/10.1093/deafed/enx023
title: Omega-is-d2: a computerized sign language-based literacy training program with Create and Test exercises, individualized starting levels, and sign-language versions of sentence material with animations
description: Omega-is-d2 is "a computerized sign language-based literacy training program that, like its forerunners, includes two types of exercises: Create and Test." In Create exercises users build sentences from word lists and see the meaning animated; in Test exercises users construct a sentence matching an animation, with positive visual feedback for correct sentences. All sentence material was translated into Swedish Sign Language, with "more than 1,700 SSL videos" recorded versus 220 in the earlier Omega-is-d1, and the animations from the original program were maintained. Materials were produced with Stockholm University's Sign Language Section and two deaf native signers.
requirements: Training starts at the level where the participant gets four out of five sentences correct in the Test exercises
A minimum of 10 min per day of use over a 4-week period was recommended in this study
constraints: Only text material from the generic program except the short stories was translated into SSL
The study recommends focusing on Create exercises, which were designed to establish connections between signed and written language
target_learners: DHH signing children who are beginning to learn to read (Grade 1 word-reading level)
target_learning_goals: Connections between sign language and written language
examples: Participants used the program in school for at least 10 min per day over 4 weeks, averaging 33 min per day, working with both Create and Test exercises
key_sources: Holmer Emil, Heimann Mikael, Rudner Mary. (2017). Computerized Sign Language-Based Literacy Training for Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Children. The Journal of Deaf Studies and Deaf Education. https://doi.org/10.1093/deafed/enx023
